1 │ # Black as color number 0 is ignored, and other wrong colors are not reported clearly
   2 │ 
   3 │ ## What happens now
   4 │ 
   5 │ When I choose a color for my text by giving the number 0, which is black, nothing happens. The text shows up with no color at all, and there is no warning that my choice was skipped. The same happens with an empty color value.
   6 │ 
   7 │ Numbers that are outside the allowed range, like 300 or a minus number, are accepted as if they were fine and end up showing nothing useful. The words true and false, when given as a color, are treated as the numbers 1 and 0 instead of being refused.
   8 │ 
   9 │ A color name that is not known does stop with a message that says the color is unknown. But a group of numbers that is the wrong shape, such as only two numbers, four numbers, or three numbers written as text, stops with a confusing internal message about too many values, too few values, or a bad format, instead of saying that the color is unknown.
  10 │ 
  11 │ ## What should happen
  12 │ 
  13 │ The number 0 should show real black for both the text color and the background color.
  14 │ 
  15 │ A value should only be accepted if it is a known color name, a whole number from 0 up to 255, or three whole numbers each from 0 up to 255.
  16 │ 
  17 │ Any other value should stop with one single, clear message that says the color is unknown. That covers empty values, unknown names, text written in capital letters, true and false, minus numbers, numbers above 255, decimal numbers, groups with the wrong count of numbers, and groups that hold text instead of numbers.
  18 │ 
  19 │ ## About this project
  20 │ 
  21 │ Click is a helper library for building command-line programs in Python. It gives people ready-made pieces such as options, prompts, progress bars, and colored output. One of those pieces lets a program put color and style on text it prints to a terminal.
  22 │ 
  23 │ ## Problem this solves
  24 │ 
  25 │ Someone who wants black text or a black background picks the lowest color number and sees nothing happen, so their carefully chosen color is lost without a word. And when they get a color value wrong, the message they see talks about the shape of the numbers rather than telling them plainly that the color is not a real color, which sends them looking in the wrong place.
  26 │ 
  27 │ ## What changed
  28 │ 
  29 │ The number 0 now shows black instead of being skipped, for both text and background.
  30 │ 
  31 │ Bad color values now all stop with the same clear message saying the color is unknown, rather than some being waved through, some being read as a number, and some failing with an internal message about the shape of the numbers.
  32 │ 
  33 │ The kind of error raised for a color that is not known is different from before, so anyone who watches for that specific error should take note.
  34 │ 
  35 │ ## Impact
  36 │ 
  37 │ Ease of use and correctness: a color that was silently dropped now works, and a wrong color now gives one clear message instead of a confusing one. There is also a small compatibility effect on the kind of error raised.
  38 │ 
  39 │ ## User experience
  40 │ 
  41 │ Before: I ask for black text by giving the color number 0 and the text comes out with no color, with no hint that my choice was ignored. After: the same number 0 turns the text black.
  42 │ 
  43 │ Before: I give only two numbers for an RGB color and get a message about not enough values to unpack. After: I get one plain message that tells me the color is unknown.

## What is missing

Nothing that the ticket asked for is missing, based on what I read:

- Black color `0` now works for both parameters: `src/click/termui.py:709` uses `if fg is not None:` and `src/click/termui.py:713` uses `if bg is not None:`, so color `0` is no longer dropped by a truthiness test.
- One clear error for bad input: `_interpret_color` at `src/click/termui.py:581` only returns for a known `str` name (line 590), an `int` in `[0, 255]` (lines 597-599), or a 3-item tuple/list of `int` channels in `[0, 255]` via `_is_rgb_channel` (line 578, lines 600-603); anything else falls through to a single `raise ValueError(_("Unknown color ..."))`. `bool` is rejected before the `int` check (lines 593-596).
- The exception-type change is documented: `CHANGES.md:18-22` describes both the `0`-color fix and the `TypeError` to `ValueError` change, and the `style` docstring carries a matching `.. versionchanged:: 8.5.0` note.

The tests in `tests/test_utils/test_style.py:81-107` cover 18 invalid values for both `fg` and `bg`, and `tests/test_utils/test_style.py:55-56` checks `{"fg": 0}` / `{"bg": 0}`; these exercise exactly the behavior the ticket describes. I did not find an existing caller in `src/` that depends on the old falsy-skip or `TypeError` behavior (`grep` for `_interpret_color` shows it used only at `src/click/termui.py:710` and `:713`).

VERDICT: approve

## Experience difference

The ticket asks for two user-visible changes, and the product that exists now delivers both.

For the first: before, passing `0` as `fg` or `bg` to `style()`/`secho()` was silently ignored, because a truthiness check treated `0` as "no color". Now `0` is a real black color, so a user who wants terminal color index 0 gets it for both foreground and background. The code at `src/click/termui.py:709` and `:713` and the checks at `tests/test_utils/test_style.py:55-56` confirm this path.

For the second: before, invalid color values raised different, confusing exceptions (`TypeError` for some types, `ValueError` for others). Now every invalid value — empty string, unknown name, wrong case, bytes, `True`/`False`, out-of-range ints like `-1` and `256`, floats, empty tuples/lists, wrong-length tuples, string channels, boolean channels, out-of-range channels — goes through one code path and raises a single `ValueError` with an `Unknown color` message. A user catching errors now only has to handle one exception type and gets one consistent message. The `CHANGES.md:18-22` entry tells users about this change, and the version note in the `style` docstring marks it as part of 8.5.0, so the change is discoverable from the docs, not just the traceback.
